question: Moulin à huile Paradis, a company based in the French department of Gard, uses artisanal, ancestral techniques to produce ‘traditional’, 100% French olive oil enjoyed by many Michelin-starred chefs. Their oil has also received several awards at the Paris International Agriculture Show’s Concours Général Agricole.

However, this year, following sensory organoleptic tests and in accordance with EU legislation, fraud monitoring services have penalised this oil by categorising it as ‘lampante oil’, making it unsuitable for sale. This decision comes at the same time that chemical tests on the same oil show that the product does conform to European standards.

The sensory tests that found the oil to be unsuitable for sale were carried out by ‘experts’ who tasted the product as part of the tests. The results therefore depended on the experts’ tastes. It would seem, therefore, that EU regulations are not adapted to local and artisanal productions that eschew industrial techniques.

Deciding whether oils can be sold solely on the basis of sensory tests when chemical tests on the same oil are positive will only lead to the disappearance of unique local characteristics. Is the Commission aware that these regulations discriminate in a way that harms artisanal companies? What measures will the Commission take to preserve the characteristics of ‘traditional’ oils?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.10.2024) Olive oil marketing standards are a part of the agricultural product quality policy. Their purpose is to take into account the expectations of consumers, to contribute to the improvement of the production and marketing of agricultural products and their quality as well as to ensure a level playing field for EU producers.

Since 1991, olive oils are categorised based on a number of parameters, including organoleptic and chemical, currently included in Regulation 2022/21041. The organoleptic characteristics are checked by panels of tasters in accordance with the International Olive Council organoleptic assessment method. Panels are approved by Member States in accordance with Article 10 of Regulation 2022/21052.

Tasters undergo regular training and panels participate in ring trials to continuously improve their performance. In addition, in accordance with Article 11 of Regulation 2022/2105, if a panel does not confirm the category declared by an operator, operators can request a counter-assessment, where the oil is assessed by two additional panels.
